lessons.title: Third down
lessons.objective: You can say why third down decides drives.

payload.prompt: Why is third down so important to both offense and defense?

options.text: It is the last chance to make a new set of downs; convert and you live, fail and the defense gets the ball
The offense always throws on third down
The defense cannot blitz on third down

explanation.correct: Exactly. Third down is the make-or-break moment. Win it and your drive continues. Lose it and you punt or go for it on fourth.
explanation.incorrect: Third down decides the drive. Convert and keep going. Stall and hand the ball to the other team.

payload.prompt: Second and eight, gain only three. What's the result?

options.label: New set of downs
options.consequence: You need ten yards to reset to first. Three yards doesn't reset the marker.
considerations: Progress counts, but only ten yards or more resets the down counter.

options.label: Third and five coming
options.consequence: After gaining three, it becomes third and five. You still need five more yards to keep the drive alive.
considerations: Down stays the same (third), yardage to gain decreases by the amount you gained.

payload.expertNote: Down and distance math is simple: yards gained reduce yardage needed. You only reset to first down when you reach or exceed the ten-yard marker.

payload.prompt: On third and long, the defense can call any coverage knowing the offense probably needs to throw. True or false?

scene.alt: A defense stacking coverage players deep on third and long yardage, preventing deep completions.

explanation.correct: True. Third and long is a passing down where the defense can gear up for a throw and leave run support for help.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, when the yard marker is far away, defenses stack pass coverage because they know a throw is coming.

payload.prompt: Match each third-down yardage to the call the defense might make.

pairs.definition: Defense stacks the box to stop a sneak or short run; the offense could go for it.
A balanced call, could be run or pass; defense watches for play-action.
Passing down; defense plays tight coverage on receivers and may not worry about the run.

explanation.summary: Third down yardage tells both teams a lot: short means sneak or dive; medium could go either way; long means throw.
explanation.sayThisLine: Third and short: stuff the box. Third and long: guard the receiver.

payload.prompt: A team with a great third-down conversion rate is usually which?

options.text: Good offensively; they move the ball and keep drives alive
Losing a lot because their offense is on the field too much
Bad at defense because third down happens all the time

explanation.correct: Converting third down is an offensive skill. High third-down conversion rate means your offense extends drives and scores.
explanation.incorrect: Third-down efficiency is an offensive stat. Convert third downs and your offense gets more chances to score.

payload.prompt: Arrange these plays in order of desperation on third down.

items.text: Third and one: sneak or dive
Third and four: power run or quick pass
Third and twelve: deep route or screen to save yards
Third and goal from the two: goal-line package

explanation.correct: Third and short is almost automatic. Third and goal is urgent. Third and long is near punt territory.
explanation.incorrect: Match the yardage to how desperate the situation is: short is safe, long is urgent.

lessons.title: Go for it?
lessons.objective: You can weigh a fourth-down decision the way fans do.

payload.prompt: Fourth and two at the 35. Down three, two minutes. Go?

options.label: Go for it
options.consequence: Aggressive but modern. Convert and you're near the goal. Fail and give the ball away.
considerations: Down 3 with time running out requires a touchdown.
Field goal makes it one-point down, still requiring another score.
Analytics favor going for it on fourth and two.

options.label: Kick field goal
options.consequence: Makes it one point down, but you still need another score. Gamble on overtime or a second drive.
considerations: Safer play but leaves you behind.

options.label: Punt
options.consequence: Gives the other team possession when you need to score. Wastes time.
considerations: Punting surrenders the ball late in the game.

payload.expertNote: Late-game math changes everything. You need a touchdown anyway, so going for it on fourth and short is the modern, mathematically sound choice.

payload.prompt: A team that converts fourth down 50 percent of the time on fourth and two has roughly what win probability?

explanation.correct: Fifty-fifty on fourth and two means you likely get the first down and keep the drive alive. That raises your win odds above 50 percent.
explanation.incorrect: Fourth and two is a high-convert situation; 50 percent success implies you are doing well.

payload.prompt: Which is NOT a factor in a fourth-down decision?

options.text: The score and time left
Your team's record and jersey colors
Field position and the opponent's strength

explanation.correct: Jersey colors do not matter in fourth-down math. Score, time, field position, and matchups do.
explanation.incorrect: Fourth-down decisions depend on the game situation and your team's ability on fourth and short, not what they are wearing.

payload.prompt: Modern analytics say coaches should go for it on fourth and short early in the game, not just at the end. True or false?

scene.alt: A coach pointing to analytics sheets showing fourth-down win probability.

explanation.correct: True. Analytics shows that going for it on fourth and one or two any time is better for win probability than punting.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, modern coaches use data to go for it earlier in games, not just when desperate.

payload.prompt: Match each situation to the fourth-down call.

pairs.term: Fourth and goal at the two
pairs.definition: Go for it; stopping a goal-line stand is what defenses are built for.
Likely punt; four yards is too far to count on, and you give up the ball way ahead.

pairs.term: Fourth and two with two minutes down three
pairs.definition: Go for it; you need a touchdown anyway and might recover an onside kick.

explanation.summary: Field position and game situation decide most fourth-down calls. Goal line and end game favor going for it.
explanation.sayThisLine: Goal line: go for it. Midfield: punt. Late and close: be aggressive.

payload.prompt: The old saying was always punt on fourth down except at the goal line. Why has that changed?

options.text: Coaches are younger and more aggressive
Data shows going for it on fourth and one or two improves win probability
The rules changed and fourth down is easier now

explanation.correct: Analytics and math changed the game. Going for it on fourth and short wins more games than punting.
explanation.incorrect: The rules stayed the same, but the math is new. Win probability favors aggressive fourth-down calls.

lessons.title: The red zone
lessons.objective: You can explain why scoring gets harder near the goal line.

payload.prompt: Why is it harder to score once the ball reaches the red zone?

options.text: The field is shorter, so routes are compressed and defenders can play tighter coverage
The defense is allowed to use more players
The quarterback has less time to throw

explanation.correct: The red zone is tight. Receivers have less room to separate, and the end zone is only ten yards deep, so deep shots become tougher.
explanation.incorrect: The red zone (inside the 20) compresses every route. You can not throw deep balls and receivers can not separate easily in that space.

payload.prompt: Tap the red zone on this field.

diagram.alt: A football field showing yard lines from the offense's perspective, with the opponent's end zone at the top and the 20-yard line marked.

explanation.correct: The red zone is from your team's attack down to inside the opponent's 20-yard line. Inside the 20, the end zone is close and cramped.
explanation.incorrect: The red zone is inside the opponent's 20. That is where field goals become easier but touchdowns get tougher because there is no room.

payload.prompt: The red zone is why field goals are so common inside the 20. True or false?

scene.alt: An offense in the red zone settling for a field goal instead of pushing for a touchdown.

explanation.correct: True. Getting to the red zone is half the battle; getting in the end zone is half of that. Field goals are the safety net.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, the red zone is where defenses tighten up and offenses often settle for three points instead of six.

payload.prompt: You are in the red zone at the opponent's 15 with three tries left. Do you run the ball or throw?

choices.text: Run the ball; limited space makes throws risky
Take the field goal and settle for three

explanation.correct: In the red zone, runs are often safer than passes because the field is too tight for receivers to create separation.
explanation.incorrect: The red zone favors the run when you are close. Deep passes are harder in a compressed field.

payload.prompt: Match each zone to what it means for scoring.

pairs.definition: Inside the opponent's 20-yard line; where every yard matters and defenses tighten up.
Right at the end zone boundary; the toughest one to cross but worth six points.
Roughly inside the 35; kickers make most attempts from here, so take the three if uncertain.

explanation.summary: The closer to the end zone, the harder it gets to move the ball but the bigger the payoff.
explanation.sayThisLine: Red zone: harder field position. Goal line: hardest defense. Field goal range: easy three.

payload.prompt: In the red zone, the defense has the advantage because?

options.text: Less field to defend; coverage is tighter and receivers have nowhere to hide
The offense is not allowed to use running backs
The defense gets an extra player for red zone plays

explanation.correct: The red zone is small, which is why defenses play better there. Receivers can not get separation and plays are compressed.
explanation.incorrect: The red zone compresses everything. Every route is covered tight and separation is impossible, so defenses thrive.

lessons.title: Kick or go for two
lessons.objective: You can explain when a team goes for two.

payload.prompt: You just scored a touchdown down by 8 points with 3 minutes left. Kick the extra point or go for two?

choices.text: Kick for one; you still need another score
Go for two; if you get it you are only down two and tied in scoring

explanation.correct: You are down 8. Kicking makes it 8 minus 7 equals 1 point down. Going for two makes it 8 minus 8 equals tied. Going for two is the call.
explanation.incorrect: Math matters on two-point decisions. Down 8, you go for two to catch the lead instead of staying down.

payload.prompt: Going for two is always a fifty-fifty gamble and never a good idea early in the game. True or false?

scene.alt: A short-yardage play from the two-yard line where the offense attempts a two-point conversion.

explanation.correct: False. From the two-yard line, teams convert two-point plays about 52 percent of the time, better than 50-50. Early analytics may favor going for two even at friendly scores.
explanation.incorrect: Two-point conversions from the two are slightly above 50-50 odds, so they are not always bad math.

payload.prompt: Which situation is the BEST for going for two?

options.text: You are up by 10 with 30 seconds left
You are down by 7 late in the game and just scored
You are tied with five minutes left

explanation.correct: Down 7, you go for two because making it ties the game. Kicking leaves you down one and needing another possession.
explanation.incorrect: Down by 7, going for two makes math sense: get it and you are tied. Kick and you stay down.

payload.prompt: Complete this sentence about two-point decisions.
payload.template: A team down {{score}} after a touchdown might go for two because {{reason}}.

options: kicking leaves them still down and needing more scoring
two points is close to five
gaps.correct: kicking leaves them still down and needing more scoring

explanation.correct: Down 5 after a touchdown, kicking makes it 5 minus 7 equals down 2. Going for two makes it 5 minus 8 equals down 3, same math either way.
explanation.incorrect: The two-point decision is about game math: does kicking leave you in a winning position or do you need to go for it?

payload.prompt: Match each scoring option after a touchdown to its reward.

pairs.definition: Snap from the 15-yard line; a 33-yard kick; nearly automatic and usually safe.
Snap from the 2-yard line; run or pass; 52 percent success from the two; two points if good.
Go for two only when the math demands it: trailing by odd scores (3, 5, 7, etc.)

explanation.summary: Extra points are safe. Two-point tries are risky but sometimes necessary for game math.
explanation.sayThisLine: Kick it: one point, almost always. Go for two: two points, risky, only when you need it.

payload.prompt: You are down 4 points and just scored a touchdown with one minute left. Kick or go for two?

options.text: Kick to make it down 3 and chase one more score
Go for two; if you get it you are only down 2
Kick and try an onside kick

explanation.correct: Down 4, kicking makes it 4 minus 7 equals down 3. You get the ball back with one minute; one more score wins. Kick for one.
explanation.incorrect: Down 4 favors kicking one because you are likely to get the ball back with time for another possession.

lessons.title: Two-minute drill
lessons.objective: You can describe how a team saves the clock.

payload.prompt: Arrange these plays in the order an offense might call them on a two-minute drive needing a touchdown.

items.text: Deep pass to the sideline to get out of bounds
Check down to the running back for a safer gain
Call timeout or spike the ball to stop the clock
Short pass inside the 20 to set up a field goal or two-point try

explanation.correct: The two-minute drill is a balance: gain yards with sideline throws and checkdowns, spike to save time, and get close enough for a score.
explanation.incorrect: In the two-minute drill, you gain yards quickly and save the clock with out-of-bounds plays and timeouts.

payload.prompt: You are at the opponent's 30 with 1:45 left and no timeouts. One incomplete pass and the clock runs to 1:30. How much time did that play cost?

explanation.correct: Incomplete passes stop the clock briefly, but the play clock runs the snap to the incompletion. That is roughly 15 seconds.
explanation.incorrect: Each play burns about 15 seconds in the two-minute drill, whether you gain yards or not.

payload.prompt: In the two-minute drill, why are sideline routes better than middle routes?

options.text: Sideline routes let the receiver step out of bounds to stop the clock
Sideline routes confuse the defense
Middle routes take more time to develop

explanation.correct: Sideline routes let the receiver step out of bounds, which stops the clock immediately. That saves precious seconds.
explanation.incorrect: Out of bounds stops the clock in the two-minute drill. Sideline throws set that up.

payload.prompt: You are at the opponent's 40 with 1:00 left, down 3, and one timeout left. Spike or call timeout first?

choices.text: Spike the ball to stop the clock, then throw on the next play
Call timeout now and save the spike for later

explanation.correct: Spike first: it costs no timeout and stops the clock. Save the timeout for after a play if you need to regroup or discuss strategy.
explanation.incorrect: The spike is free; it stops the clock and does not cost a timeout. Use it first, then save your timeout for a crucial moment.

payload.prompt: The quarterback can spike the ball on any down, including third down, to stop the clock. True or false?

scene.alt: A quarterback spiking the ball after an incomplete pass in the two-minute drill.

explanation.correct: True. A spike is a legal play: it is an incomplete forward pass that stops the clock and counts as a down.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, the quarterback can spike the ball on any down. It is an incomplete pass that costs a down.

payload.prompt: Match each two-minute tool to what it does.

pairs.definition: A route where the receiver can step out of bounds to stop the clock instantly.
The quarterback throws the ball on the ground to stop the clock and reset; costs a down.
Stops the clock for one minute to regroup; each team gets three per half.

explanation.summary: The two-minute drill is about managing every second. Sidelines, spikes and timeouts are your weapons.
explanation.sayThisLine: Sideline stops the clock. Spike stops the clock. Timeout stops the clock. Use them all.

lessons.title: Managing the clock
lessons.objective: You can spot good and bad clock management.

payload.prompt: You are winning by 3 and the other team has the ball with 1:30 left at midfield, one timeout. What clock play helps you win?

choices.text: Let them throw quickly and save the clock
Make them run the ball so the clock keeps running

explanation.correct: Force them to run because the clock runs faster on running plays. Pass plays stop the clock on incompletions.
explanation.incorrect: You want to run down the clock. Make them run the ball so the clock moves faster.

payload.prompt: When ahead, you want the offense to use quick plays and move fast to burn the clock. True or false?

scene.alt: An offense running the ball to run down the clock while ahead in the game.

explanation.correct: False. When ahead, you want slow, methodical drives. Run the ball, take your time, use the whole play clock.
explanation.incorrect: No, when you are ahead you want to slow the pace. Run the ball and use the full 40-second play clock.

payload.prompt: When trailing late, what is the worst clock mistake?

options.text: Running the ball instead of passing and stopping the clock with incompletions
Throwing sideline routes to get out of bounds
Taking a timeout between plays

explanation.correct: Running wastes time when trailing. Passing stops the clock on incompletions and sideline throws stop it on contact.
explanation.incorrect: Trailing late? You need stops to save the clock. Pass plays with sideline routes are clock-savers.

statement.speaker: Broadcast analyst
statement.text: They are running the victory formation now. The game is basically over.

payload.question: What is happening?

options.text: The winning team is celebrating early
The winning team is kneeling down to run out the final seconds safely
There is a formation advantage for the ahead team
The offense is changing strategy for the last play

payload.translation: Victory formation is the kneel-down: the quarterback takes the snap and drops to a knee to waste time and avoid a costly turnover.

followUps.line: Why not run the ball for yards in victory formation?
followUps.why: Shows you know clock management: kneeling is about running time, not gaining yards.

followUps.line: Can the defense stop a victory formation play?
followUps.why: Tests your sense that kneeling is unstoppable when ahead.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask why a team would give up the chance to score more points when ahead.

payload.prompt: Match each clock situation to the right strategy.

pairs.definition: Run the ball, use the full play clock, burn timeouts by stopping short of the sticks.
Pass quickly, throw sidelines to stop the clock, use timeouts to regroup only when needed.
Kneel down to waste the final seconds safely without risking a fumble or turnover.

explanation.summary: Clock management is opposite depending on the score. Ahead: slow it down. Behind: speed it up. Won: just kneel.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ahead: run and waste time. Behind: pass and save time. Up by a ton: kneel down.

payload.prompt: Using a timeout to stop the clock is valuable when?

options.text: You are trailing and need to regroup to design a crucial third-down play or two-minute situation
You are ahead and want to slow the game pace
You want to stop the other team from running the clock

explanation.correct: Timeouts are best used when trailing to save time and regroup. Wasting timeouts when ahead is a clock-management mistake.
explanation.incorrect: Timeouts matter most when trailing and in a hurry. When ahead, avoid using them and let the game tick down.

lessons.title: Overtime
lessons.objective: You can explain how overtime works and who gets the ball.

payload.prompt: In NFL regular-season overtime as of 2025, what changed?

options.text: Each team gets a possession, not just first-score wins
Overtime is now five minutes instead of ten
Field goals do not count in overtime

explanation.correct: Since 2025, both teams get at least one possession in NFL regular-season OT, like the playoffs. First-score no longer wins automatically.
explanation.incorrect: The 2025 rule change let both teams get the ball in overtime. It applies to regular season now too.

payload.prompt: Arrange these overtime scenarios by which team wins first.

items.text: Receiving team scores a touchdown on their first drive
Receiving team scores a field goal, then defending team scores a touchdown
Both teams score field goals, then one team scores a touchdown
Both teams score two field goals each

explanation.correct: In modern overtime, each team gets the ball at least once. Whoever scores the most wins, regardless of order.
explanation.incorrect: Since both teams get a possession, the game ends when one team has more points after both have had a chance.

payload.prompt: The coin flip winner gets the ball in OT. Should they take the ball or defer?

choices.text: Take the ball and score first for a sudden-death advantage
Defer so the other team scores first and you know what you need

explanation.correct: With both teams getting a possession, deferring is smart. Let them score first, then you know exactly what you need to tie or win.
explanation.incorrect: The 2025 change means deferring is often the better call. You get the last possession and know the situation.

payload.prompt: Sudden-death overtime means the first team to score any points wins. True or false?

scene.alt: An overtime game where one team scores and the game ends immediately.

explanation.correct: False. In NFL OT now, both teams get a possession. The team with more points after both possessions wins, not sudden-death.
explanation.incorrect: Modern overtime is not sudden-death anymore. Both teams get the ball, then whoever has more points wins.

payload.prompt: Match each overtime format to how it works.

pairs.definition: Each team gets at least one possession; the team with more points after both have the ball wins.
Same as regular season: both teams get the ball; touchdown wins if the other team cannot answer.
Each team gets one untimed possession from the 25-yard line; alternating until one team wins.

explanation.summary: NFL OT is now fair: both teams get the ball. College OT is a shootout. Playoff OT has sudden-death rules.
explanation.sayThisLine: NFL both teams get the ball. College is a shootout. Playoffs have sudden-death.

payload.prompt: Getting the ball second in NFL overtime is now an advantage because?

options.text: You know the score and can plan accordingly; if they score, you can match or beat them
The defense is tired from the first possession
The second team always gets a two-point conversion

explanation.correct: Knowing what you need before you score is huge. Go second, see their result, then execute with a plan.
explanation.incorrect: The second possession in modern OT has the information advantage: you know the score before your drive.
